claim: Old mice (18-22 months) contain fewer CD4+ T-cells compared with adult mice (8-12 weeks).
source: We report that, while old mice (18–22 months) contain fewer CD4+ T-cells compared with adults (8–12 weeks), those that remain have a higher intrinsic affinity for self-pMHC, as measured by CD5 expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing total CD4+ T-cell numbers between adult and old mice.

claim: CD4+ T-cells in old mice have a higher intrinsic affinity for self-pMHC as measured by CD5 expression.
source: We report that, while old mice (18–22 months) contain fewer CD4+ T-cells compared with adults (8–12 weeks), those that remain have a higher intrinsic affinity for self-pMHC, as measured by CD5 expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating increased CD5 expression on CD4+ T-cells from old mice.

claim: Old mice have more cells that bind individual or multiple distinct foreign-pMHCs.
source: Old mice also have more cells that bind individual or multiple distinct foreign-pMHCs, and the fold increase in pMHC-binding populations is directly related to their CD5 levels.
evidence: Supported by tetramer enrichment data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating increased numbers of pMHC-binding cells in old mice.

claim: The fold increase in pMHC-binding populations is directly related to their CD5 levels.
source: Old mice also have more cells that bind individual or multiple distinct foreign-pMHCs, and the fold increase in pMHC-binding populations is directly related to their CD5 levels.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A,B demonstrating the relationship between CD5 levels and fold change in tetramer-positive populations.

claim: The CD4+ T-cell compartment preferentially accumulates promiscuous constituents with age as a consequence of higher affinity T-cell receptor interactions with self-pMHC.
source: These data demonstrate that the CD4+ T-cell compartment preferentially accumulates promiscuous constituents with age as a consequence of higher affinity T-cell receptor interactions with self-pMHC.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings including CD5 expression data, tetramer binding data, and correlation analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Thymic development limits clonal representation to T-cells bearing TCRs within an affinity window for self-pMHC.
source: Thymic development limits clonal representation to T-cells bearing TCRs within an affinity window for self-pMHC (Savage and Davis, 2001; Yin et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2014), while peripheral space physically constrains the number of T-cells present to recognize foreign-pMHC (Mason, 1998; Vrisekoop et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Peripheral space physically constrains the number of T-cells present to recognize foreign-pMHC.
source: Thymic development limits clonal representation to T-cells bearing TCRs within an affinity window for self-pMHC (Savage and Davis, 2001; Yin et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2014), while peripheral space physically constrains the number of T-cells present to recognize foreign-pMHC (Mason, 1998; Vrisekoop et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Aging is associated with increased susceptibility to infections and decreased responsiveness to vaccines.
source: Aging is associated with increased susceptibility to infections and decreased responsiveness to vaccines, suggesting that individual repertoires converge on a point where their diversity is insufficient to bind and/or mount a protective response to foreign-pMHC (Vazquez-Boland et al., 2001; Nichol, 2008; Nikolich-Zugich, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: TCR diversity within both the CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell compartments contract from adult to old mice in parallel with thymic involution.
source: Consistent with this idea, TCR diversity within both the CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell compartments contract from adult to old mice in parallel with thymic involution (Ahmed et al., 2009; Rudd et al., 2011; Britanova et al., 2014), and the number of CD8+ T-cells that bind distinct foreign class I pMHC in unprimed mice decreases over the lifespan (Yager et al., 2008; Rudd et al., 2011; Decman et al., 2012; Smithey et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The number of CD8+ T-cells that bind distinct foreign class I pMHC in unprimed mice decreases over the lifespan.
source: Consistent with this idea, TCR diversity within both the CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell compartments contract from adult to old mice in parallel with thymic involution (Ahmed et al., 2009; Rudd et al., 2011; Britanova et al., 2014), and the number of CD8+ T-cells that bind distinct foreign class I pMHC in unprimed mice decreases over the lifespan (Yager et al., 2008; Rudd et al., 2011; Decman et al., 2012; Smithey et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Unprimed old C57BL/6 mice have fewer CD4+ T-cells in their secondary lymphoid organs than adults due to a loss of naive (CD44lo) T-cells.
source: Unprimed old (18–22 months) C57BL/6 mice were found to have fewer CD4+ T-cells in their secondary lymphoid organs than adults (8–12 weeks) due to a loss of naive (CD44lo) T-cells, as expected given thymic involution (Figure 1A,B) (den Braber et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and consistent with prior knowledge about thymic involution.

claim: The number of memory phenotype (CD44hi) CD4+ T-cells increased with aging.
source: The number of memory phenotype (CD44hi) CD4+ T-cells increased with aging (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in memory phenotype CD4+ T-cells could be due to prior antigen experience and/or homeostatic proliferation.
source: This could be due to prior antigen experience and/or homeostatic proliferation (Nikolich-Zugich, 2008; Surh and Sprent, 2008).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CD5 expression is a surrogate for the strength of tonic TCR-pMHC interactions.
source: To assess steady-state TCR engagement, we measured CD5 expression, as a surrogate for the strength of tonic TCR–pMHC interactions (Azzam et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2001; Mandl et al., 2012, 2013; Persaud et al., 2014; Vrisekoop et al., 2014; Fulton et al., 2015); CD3 levels, which decrease upon TCR engagement (Valitutti et al., 1995); and BrdU incorporation to assess proliferation in unprimed mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work establishing CD5 as a marker of TCR-pMHC interaction strength.

claim: CD3 levels decrease upon TCR engagement.
source: To assess steady-state TCR engagement, we measured CD5 expression, as a surrogate for the strength of tonic TCR–pMHC interactions (Azzam et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2001; Mandl et al., 2012, 2013; Persaud et al., 2014; Vrisekoop et al., 2014; Fulton et al., 2015); CD3 levels, which decrease upon TCR engagement (Valitutti et al., 1995); and BrdU incorporation to assess proliferation in unprimed mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: CD5 was higher on memory CD4+ T-cells in adult mice relative to adult naive T-cells.
source: CD5 was higher on memory CD4+ T-cells in adult mice relative to adult naive T-cells, as expected (Mandl et al., 2013), while both naive and memory CD4+ T-cells in old mice had higher CD5 expression relative to adult naive cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and consistent with prior published work.

claim: Both naive and memory CD4+ T-cells in old mice had higher CD5 expression relative to adult naive cells.
source: CD5 was higher on memory CD4+ T-cells in adult mice relative to adult naive T-cells, as expected (Mandl et al., 2013), while both naive and memory CD4+ T-cells in old mice had higher CD5 expression relative to adult naive cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: An inverse relationship was observed between CD5 and CD3 levels, consistent with CD5 reflecting tonic TCR engagement.
source: An inverse relationship was observed between CD5 and CD3 levels, consistent with CD5 reflecting tonic TCR engagement (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and consistent with the known biology of CD5 and CD3.

claim: Cells with high CD5 expression incorporated the most BrdU in adult and old mice, consistent with tonic TCR interactions driving homeostatic proliferation.
source: Finally, cells with high CD5 expression incorporated the most BrdU in adult and old mice, consistent with tonic TCR interactions driving homeostatic proliferation (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and consistent with the hypothesis that TCR engagement drives proliferation.

claim: A higher frequency of BrdU+ cells was observed in old mice compared with adults.
source: A higher frequency of BrdU+ cells was observed in old mice compared with adults.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The higher frequency of BrdU+ cells in old mice did not result in significantly more BrdU+CD4+ T-cells due to the total number of CD4+ T-cells dropping in old mice.
source: However, since the total number of CD4+ T-cell drops in old mice this did not result in significantly more BrdU+CD4+ T-cells (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: The CD4+ T-cell compartment increases in clonal representation of constituents with higher intrinsic affinity for self-pMHC.
source: Altogether, the data indicate that the CD4+ T-cell compartment increases in clonal representation of constituents with higher intrinsic affinity for self-pMHC.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on CD5 expression, CD3 levels, and BrdU incorporation.

claim: WNV lethality increases over the lifespan of mice and humans.
source: I-Ab tetramers presenting an immunodominant peptide (aa 641–655) from West Nile Virus (WNV) envelope protein (E641:I-Ab) were used because WNV lethality increases over the lifespan of mice and humans, making it a useful model for investigating age-related defects in susceptibility to viral infection and vaccine efficacy (Brien et al., 2008, 2009; Uhrlaub et al., 2011; Suthar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Two-color tetramer enrichment revealed more cells binding E641:I-Ab in old mice than adults.
source: Two-color tetramer enrichment (Nelson et al., 2015) revealed more cells binding E641:I-Ab in old mice than adults (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: OVA:I-Ab was considered to be subdominant because immunization with OVA elicited a smaller response than E641 in isolation and failed to mount a response upon co-immunization with E641.
source: OVA:I-Ab was considered to be subdominant because immunization with OVA elicited a smaller response than E641 in isolation and failed to mount a response upon co-immunization with E641 (Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 4.

claim: OVA:I-Ab monomer is less SDS-stable than E641:I-Ab at room temperature.
source: OVA:I-Ab monomer is also less SDS-stable than E641:I-Ab at room temperature (not shown), and pMHC stability is directly related to immunodominance (Lazarski et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated as an observation (though data not shown) and supported by citation linking pMHC stability to immunodominance.

claim: pMHC stability is directly related to immunodominance.
source: OVA:I-Ab monomer is also less SDS-stable than E641:I-Ab at room temperature (not shown), and pMHC stability is directly related to immunodominance (Lazarski et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Alloreactive cells are likely to be selected on a broader range of self-pMHC and represent a broader subset of the CD4+ T-cell compartment.
source: Alloreactive cells were enumerated because they are likely to be selected on a broader range of self-pMHC and represent a broader subset of the CD4+ T-cell compartment (Felix and Allen, 2007; Chu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: His-tag enrichment yielded more E641-bound adult cells than anti-PE/APC beads.
source: This yielded more E641-bound adult cells than the anti-PE/APC beads (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing enrichment methods shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Tetramers cannot detect all CD4+ T-cells that respond to a given class II pMHC via weak TCR-pMHC interactions.
source: Since tetramers cannot detect all CD4+ T-cells that respond to a given class II pMHC via weak TCR–pMHC interactions (Sabatino et al., 2011), the more avid His-tag enrichment is likely to detect T-cells that bind tetramers with lower avidity.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work and logical inference about the His-tag enrichment method.

claim: The more avid His-tag enrichment is likely to detect T-cells that bind tetramers with lower avidity.
source: Since tetramers cannot detect all CD4+ T-cells that respond to a given class II pMHC via weak TCR–pMHC interactions (Sabatino et al., 2011), the more avid His-tag enrichment is likely to detect T-cells that bind tetramers with lower avidity.
evidence: Logical inference based on the properties of the His-tag enrichment method.

claim: More naive and memory cells were observed to bind a single pMHC specificity in old mice compared with adults when using dump tetramer gating.
source: More naive and memory cells were observed to bind a single pMHC specificity in old mice compared with adults when using dump tetramer gating (Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplements 5, 6) (Savage et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplements 5, 6.

claim: Since CD4+ T-cells decline with aging, those that are left appear to bind foreign pMHC more promiscuously.
source: This indicates that the increase in CD4+ T-cells binding E641:I-Ab is not unique. Rather, since CD4+ T-cells decline with aging, those that are left appear to bind foreign pMHC more promiscuously.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that multiple pMHC specificities show increased binding in old mice despite overall decline in CD4+ T-cell numbers.

claim: The number of naive cells binding OVA+MCC was higher in old mice compared with adults.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the number of naive cells binding OVA+MCC was higher in old mice compared with adults, as were the number of memory cells binding E641+OVA or OVA+MCC (Figure 2J–L and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J–L and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–9.

claim: The number of memory cells binding E641+OVA or OVA+MCC was higher in old mice compared with adults.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the number of naive cells binding OVA+MCC was higher in old mice compared with adults, as were the number of memory cells binding E641+OVA or OVA+MCC (Figure 2J–L and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J–L and Figure 2—figure supplements 7–9.

claim: The CD4+ T-cell compartment becomes polyspecific over time.
source: Altogether, these data provide evidence that the CD4+ T-cell compartment becomes polyspecific over time.
evidence: Inferred from the combined tetramer binding data showing increased binding to multiple pMHC specificities in old mice.

claim: The frequency of E641-bound CD4 single positive (SP) cells was higher for old thymocytes compared with the adults.
source: The frequency of E641-bound CD4 single positive (SP) cells was higher for old thymocytes compared with the adults, while the frequency of OVA and MCC-bound CD4SPs did not differ (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequency of OVA and MCC-bound CD4SPs did not differ between adult and old thymocytes.
source: The frequency of E641-bound CD4 single positive (SP) cells was higher for old thymocytes compared with the adults, while the frequency of OVA and MCC-bound CD4SPs did not differ (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD4SPs binding two distinct tetramers were not detected amongst the small number of tetramer-enriched samples.
source: CD4SPs binding two distinct tetramers were not detected amongst the small number of tetramer-enriched samples.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Dual binders average <10% of a peripheral population.
source: This is not surprising given that dual binders average <10% of a peripheral population (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Thymic output remains constant as a function of size over time.
source: Since thymic output remains constant as a function of size over time (Hale et al., 2006), the higher frequency of E641-bound CD4SP thymocytes in old mice suggests that more E641-binders leave the thymus of old mice than adults on a daily basis.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The higher frequency of E641-bound CD4SP thymocytes in old mice suggests that more E641-binders leave the thymus of old mice than adults on a daily basis.
source: Since thymic output remains constant as a function of size over time (Hale et al., 2006), the higher frequency of E641-bound CD4SP thymocytes in old mice suggests that more E641-binders leave the thymus of old mice than adults on a daily basis.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of constant thymic output and higher frequency of E641-bound CD4SP cells in old mice.

claim: Mature CD4+ T-cells re-entering the thymus increase from ~10% in adult mice to ~20% in old mice.
source: However, mature CD4+ T-cells re-entering the thymus increase from ∼10% in adult mice to ∼20% in old mice (Hale et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Age-related changes in thymic selection impact the clonal representation and binding capacity of the CD4+ T-cell compartment.
source: Nevertheless, the data suggest that age-related changes in thymic selection impact the clonal representation and binding capacity of the CD4+ T-cell compartment.
evidence: Inferred from the thymic data showing differential frequencies of pMHC-binding CD4SP thymocytes.

claim: CD5 levels on the tetramer-bound adult populations, relative to those on the total adult CD4+ T-cell population, directly correlated with the fold increase in the absolute number of these populations over time.
source: CD5 levels on the tetramer-bound adult populations, relative to those on the total adult CD4+ T-cell population, directly correlated with the fold increase in the absolute number of these populations over time (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Steady-state BrdU incorporation for adult and old tetramer-bound CD4+ T-cells mirrored the rank order (OVA>E641>MCC) of CD5 expression seen in both the naive and memory populations.
source: Steady-state BrdU incorporation for adult and old tetramer-bound CD4+ T-cells also mirrored the rank order (OVA>E641>MCC) of CD5 expression seen in both the naive and memory populations (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: CD5 levels are predictive of the fold-increase in pMHC-specific CD4+ T-cell subsets with aging.
source: Thus, CD5 levels are predictive of the fold-increase in pMHC-specific CD4+ T-cell subsets with aging, suggesting a link between affinity for self-pMHC, homeostatic proliferation, and expansion over time.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between CD5 levels and fold change in tetramer-positive populations.

claim: There is a link between affinity for self-pMHC, homeostatic proliferation, and expansion over time.
source: Thus, CD5 levels are predictive of the fold-increase in pMHC-specific CD4+ T-cell subsets with aging, suggesting a link between affinity for self-pMHC, homeostatic proliferation, and expansion over time.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on CD5 expression, BrdU incorporation, and fold changes in tetramer-positive populations.

claim: The size of the CD4+ T-cell compartment contracts with aging but the capacity of CD4+ T-cells to bind foreign-pMHC increases over the lifespan.
source: Here, we contribute to our basic understanding of T-cell biology by reporting that the size of the CD4+ T-cell compartment contracts with aging but, unlike CD8+ T-cells, the capacity of CD4+ T-cells to bind foreign-pMHC increases over the lifespan.
evidence: Supported by the combined experimental data on CD4+ T-cell numbers and pMHC binding capacity.

claim: A decrease in cortical thymic epithelial cells and changes in antigen processing could increase competition for positively selecting pMHC.
source: A decrease in cortical thymic epithelial cells and changes in antigen processing could increase competition for positively selecting pMHC (Chinn et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2014), favoring higher TCR affinity for self-pMHC.
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increased competition for positively selecting pMHC favors higher TCR affinity for self-pMHC.
source: A decrease in cortical thymic epithelial cells and changes in antigen processing could increase competition for positively selecting pMHC (Chinn et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2014), favoring higher TCR affinity for self-pMHC.
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Decreased expression of TRAs on fewer medullary TECs could lead to competition for negatively selecting pMHC with aging.
source: In addition, decreased expression of TRAs on fewer medullary TECs (Chinn et al., 2012; Griffith et al., 2012) could lead to competition for negatively selecting pMHC with aging.
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Experimentally limiting thymic selection differentially impacts the CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell compartments, with CD4+ T-cells becoming more polyspecific and CD8+ T-cells becoming more pMHC focused.
source: Experimentally limiting thymic selection differentially impacts the CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell compartments, with CD4+ T-cells becoming more polyspecific and CD8+ T-cells becoming more pMHC focused (Huseby et al., 2005; Chu et al., 2009, 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Age-related changes in the thymus would be expected to restrict negative selection and result in a CD4+ T-cell compartment with a broader binding capacity.
source: Thus, age-related changes in the thymus would be expected to restrict negative selection and result in a CD4+ T-cell compartment with a broader binding capacity, as observed here.
evidence: Inferred from prior knowledge about thymic selection and the experimental observations in this study.

claim: T-cells can productively rearrange two TCRα subunits and express two TCRs that increase reactivity to self- and allo-pMHC.
source: It is also noteworthy that T-cells can productively rearrange two TCRα subunits and express two TCRs that increase reactivity to self- and allo-pMHC (Ni et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Whether T-cells expressing two TCRs increase over time remains unexplored.
source: Whether T-cells expressing two TCRs increase over time remains unexplored.
evidence: Stated as an open question.

claim: A link between higher affinity for self-pMHC and residence within the CD4+ T-cell memory pool of adult mice was previously reported.
source: A link between higher affinity for self-pMHC and residence within the CD4+ T-cell memory pool of adult mice was previously reported (Mandl et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Affinity for self-pMHC influences clonal fitness over time.
source: Here, we extended this observation to naive and memory CD4+ T-cells in old mice, indicating that affinity for self-pMHC influences clonal fitness over time.
evidence: Inferred from the extension of prior observations to old mice in this study.

claim: The relationship between affinity for self-pMHC and clonal fitness over time is akin to the affinity of TCR-pMHC interactions influencing clonal fitness within a polyclonal response to cognate antigens.
source: This would be akin to the affinity of TCR–pMHC interactions influencing clonal fitness within a polyclonal response to cognate antigens (Lanzavecchia and Sallusto, 2002; Gett et al., 2003; Malherbe et al., 2004).
evidence: Analogy supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CD5 levels on adult tetramer-binding memory subsets directly correlated with their fold expansion over the lifespan.
source: Indeed, CD5 levels on adult tetramer-binding memory subsets directly correlated with their fold expansion over the lifespan showing that CD5 levels have a clear predictive value when identifying populations with a long-term advantage for clonal representation within the CD4+ T-cell compartment.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: CD5 levels have a clear predictive value when identifying populations with a long-term advantage for clonal representation within the CD4+ T-cell compartment.
source: Indeed, CD5 levels on adult tetramer-binding memory subsets directly correlated with their fold expansion over the lifespan showing that CD5 levels have a clear predictive value when identifying populations with a long-term advantage for clonal representation within the CD4+ T-cell compartment.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between CD5 levels and fold expansion.

claim: The relationship between CD4+ T cells and immune senescence is more complex than has been reported for CD8+ T cells.
source: Altogether, the data presented here suggest a more complex relationship between CD4+ T cells and immune senescence than has been reported for the CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting findings between CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells regarding pMHC binding capacity with age.

claim: An increase in binding capacity may compensate for a decrease in total CD4+ T cell numbers.
source: While an increase in binding capacity may compensate for a decrease in total CD4+ T cell numbers, the consequences of this increase remain unclear.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: A population with a higher affinity for self-pMHC and broader binding capacity poses obvious risks that could explain the increase in age-related autoimmune diseases.
source: Certainly, a population with a higher affinity for self-pMHC and broader binding capacity poses obvious risks that could explain the increase in age-related autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and giant cell arteritis (Weyand et al., 2003; Mohan et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to prior work on age-related autoimmune diseases.

claim: Old male C57BL/6 mice (18-22 months) were obtained from the National Institute of Aging breeding colony.
source: Old (18–22 months) male C57BL/6 mice were obtained from the National Institute of Aging breeding colony Bethesda, MD.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Adult male C57BL/6 mice (8-12 weeks) were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory.
source: Adult (8–12 weeks) male C57BL/6 mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory Bar Harbor, Maine.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Class II pMHC monomers were generated with baculovirus expression vectors based on pAcGP67A encoding acidic or basic leucine zippers.
source: Class II pMHC monomers were generated with baculovirus expression vectors, based on pAcGP67A (BD Pharmingen San Jose, CA), encoding acidic or basic leucine zippers (generous gift of KC Garcia) according to the approach of Teyton and colleagues (Scott et al., 1996).
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail with citation to the approach used.

claim: Two-color tetramer enrichment and gating for a single pMHC specificity was performed as a method for reducing false-positives in tetramer analysis.
source: Two-color tetramer enrichment and gating for a single pMHC specificity was performed as a method for reducing false-positives in tetramer analysis (Stetson et al., 2002; Obar et al., 2008; Nelson et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated as a methodological approach with citations to prior work.

claim: Cells which bind to tetramers via TCR-pMHC interactions will fall on a diagonal in two-color analysis, while those that bind to the fluorescent protein in a TCR-independent manner should fall off the diagonal.
source: The operating principle followed here is that cells which bind to tetramers via TCR–pMHC interactions will fall on a diagonal, since binding should be proportional for each, while those that bind to the FP in a TCR-independent manner should fall off the diagonal (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 3).
evidence: Stated as the operating principle of the two-color tetramer method.
